explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God says Aaron and his four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, are to serve Him as priests (Exodus 28:1). Aaron is Moses' brother, and the whole job here is serving God. I'd call that a family business.

Close to a job title, but not the one God gives. He says Aaron and his sons are brought "to serve Me as priests" (Exodus 28:1). Nobody here is sitting behind a bench with a gavel. The whole outfit that follows is for priests.

Nice crown energy, friend, but no. God says Aaron and his four sons are brought to serve Him "as priests" (Exodus 28:1). Moses isn't handing out thrones here. He's getting ready to dress a priesthood.
Right on the money. God says to make holy garments for Aaron "to give him glory and splendor" (Exodus 28:2). These aren't just work clothes. They're meant to look the part.
I get it, friend. Most of us hear 'clothes' and think of sweatpants. But God says the garments are "to give him glory and splendor" (Exodus 28:2). Nothing in the text mentions comfort.

Strong guess, but not what the verse says. God says these holy garments are "to give him glory and splendor" (Exodus 28:2). Strength and courage do show up elsewhere in Scripture, just not in this verse.

Yes, friend. God tells Moses to instruct "all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom" to make Aaron's garments (Exodus 28:3). Moses gives the instructions and the craftsmen do the stitching. That's a relief for everybody who has seen how I handle thread.

Good thought, but the text doesn't say that. God tells Moses to instruct "all the skilled craftsmen" to make the garments (Exodus 28:3). The Levites aren't named for this job. The sewing goes to the people God filled with a spirit of wisdom.

Tempting, since the garments are for them too. But God points Moses to someone else: "all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom" (Exodus 28:3). Aaron's sons are on the receiving end here, not at the sewing table.

Not quite, friend. God says they make these holy garments "for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests" (Exodus 28:4). So the garments aren't for Aaron alone. His sons get dressed for the job too.

That's right. The text says they make these holy garments "for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests" (Exodus 28:4). So Aaron isn't the only one getting dressed up. His sons are in the wardrobe plan too.
Yes, sir, yes, ma'am. God says to engrave on the two onyx stones "the names of the sons of Israel" (Exodus 28:9). That's the family the nation came from. Their names go right on the priest's clothes.
I see where you're going, friend, but that's not in the verse. God says to engrave "the names of the sons of Israel" on the stones (Exodus 28:9). It's the sons of Israel, not a list of elders.
Not this time, friend. The verse says to engrave on the stones "the names of the sons of Israel" (Exodus 28:9). No judges are mentioned anywhere in these instructions.
That's it. Six names go on one stone and six on the other, "in the order of their birth" (Exodus 28:10). Oldest to youngest, no cutting in line. Everybody gets their spot.
Reasonable guess, friend, but the text goes another way. The names go on the stones "in the order of their birth" (Exodus 28:10). Nobody gets bumped up a stone for a fancier title.
Ha, nobody's checking bank accounts here. God says the names go on the two stones "in the order of their birth" (Exodus 28:10). Money doesn't come into it.

Not quite, friend. The two onyx stones are fastened "on the shoulder pieces of the ephod" (Exodus 28:12). The turban comes up later, and what goes on its front is a gold plate (Exodus 28:36-37). The stones ride on his shoulders.

Right. The stones are fastened "on the shoulder pieces of the ephod" (Exodus 28:12). Aaron's turban is a different piece, and what goes on the front of it is a gold plate (Exodus 28:36-37). So these stones sit on his shoulders.

That's the word, friend. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders "as a memorial before the LORD" (Exodus 28:12). Twelve names, carried on his shoulders every time he serves. That's a whole family on his back, and I think it must feel like carrying a full cookie tray.

I love the shine in that guess, friend, but no. Aaron bears their names on his shoulders "as a memorial before the LORD" (Exodus 28:12). A crown would sit on a head. This one is carried on the shoulders as a memorial.

Good fighting spirit, friend, but the verse doesn't say shield. Aaron is to bear their names on his shoulders "as a memorial before the LORD" (Exodus 28:12). The stones are there to remember the sons of Israel.

Yep. God says to make the breastpiece "with the same workmanship as the ephod" and to build it with gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and fine linen (Exodus 28:15). It matches the ephod. Same fine work, same materials.

Not this time, friend. God says the breastpiece is made "with the same workmanship as the ephod," with gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and fine linen (Exodus 28:15). It's a match with the ephod, and the materials are the same.
Square it is. The breastpiece "must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide" (Exodus 28:16). Four equal sides, nothing fancy. Even my cookie cutters would be proud.
Good try, friend, but this one has corners. God says it "must be square when folded over double" (Exodus 28:16). Round would roll right off the plan.
Oval's a nice shape, friend, but the text says otherwise. The breastpiece "must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide" (Exodus 28:16). Equal on both sides means square.
You got it. The twelve stones are "each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes" (Exodus 28:21). One stone, one tribe. Nobody gets left out.
Close in spirit, friend, but not in the text. Each stone is engraved "with the name of one of the twelve tribes" (Exodus 28:21). The stones name the tribes, not elders.

I see why you'd think that, since priests are the whole point. But each stone is engraved "with the name of one of the twelve tribes" (Exodus 28:21). The priest wears them. The names on them are the tribes.

Right over the heart. God says that in the Holy Place Aaron "shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment" (Exodus 28:29). That's a pretty close place to keep people. I think that says something.

Not on the back, friend. The verse says Aaron "shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment" (Exodus 28:29). The breastpiece sits on the front, right over the heart.
Hands are a good guess, friend, since priests do a lot of work. But the text says Aaron bears the names "over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment" (Exodus 28:29). They're worn, not held.

Not so, friend. God says Aaron bears the names over his heart "as a continual reminder before the LORD" (Exodus 28:29). Continual means it doesn't stop after day one. Whenever he enters the Holy Place, the names go with him.
Right. The text says Aaron bears the names "as a continual reminder before the LORD" whenever he enters the Holy Place (Exodus 28:29). It's not a first-day thing. It keeps going.

Yes. God says to place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece "so that they will also be over Aaron's heart whenever he comes before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30). They ride in the same spot as the names. Same place, same breastpiece.

The shoulders hold the onyx stones, friend (Exodus 28:12). The Urim and Thummim go in the breastpiece, "over Aaron's heart whenever he comes before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30). Different piece, different spot.

The forehead has its own piece, friend. That's where the gold plate goes (Exodus 28:36-38). The Urim and Thummim are placed in the breastpiece, "over Aaron's heart whenever he comes before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30).

That's the word. "Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30). It's the same word as in the breastpiece's name. Continually means he carries it every time.

I can see why that came to mind, friend, but the verse uses another word. It says Aaron "will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30). Sorrows isn't in there.

Offerings do come up in the passage, friend, but not here. The verse says Aaron "will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD" (Exodus 28:30). What he carries over his heart is the judgment.
Ding, ding. God says to make pomegranates of yarn all the way around the lower hem, "with gold bells between them" (Exodus 28:33). Pomegranate, bell, pomegranate, bell. That's a hem with a rhythm.
Not quite, friend. The verse says the pomegranates go around the lower hem "with gold bells between them" (Exodus 28:33). Silver and hooks aren't part of this robe.
Rings show up on the breastpiece, but those are gold (Exodus 28:23). On the robe's hem, the pomegranates have "gold bells between them" (Exodus 28:33). So it's bells that go in the gaps.
Yes. The robe's sound "will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD" (Exodus 28:35). Every time Aaron goes in or out, those bells ring. Nobody has to wonder whether he's there.
Good guess on the layout, friend, but the verse says something else. The sound "will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD" (Exodus 28:35). The word is sanctuary.

The camp is a bit far from the action, friend. The verse says the sound "will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD" (Exodus 28:35). It's the sanctuary that gets the bell sound.

That's right. God says Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers, and its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary, "so that he will not die" (Exodus 28:35). That's a serious line, and I'd say it's worth a quiet moment. God means these instructions to be followed.

It's a heavy one, friend, but it is in the text. God says the robe's sound will be heard when Aaron enters or exits the sanctuary, "so that he will not die" (Exodus 28:35). So the instructions about the robe and its sound do come with that reason.
That's the one. God tells Moses to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it "as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD" (Exodus 28:36). Four words, gold plate, right on the priest. Hard to miss.
That's a true line from Scripture, friend, but it's not the one for this plate (Deuteronomy 6:4). Here God says to engrave "HOLY TO THE LORD" (Exodus 28:36). This plate carries those words.
A fine thing to say, friend, but it's not the engraving. God says to engrave on the gold plate "HOLY TO THE LORD" (Exodus 28:36). Those are the words that go on it.

Yes, friend. God says, "Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban" (Exodus 28:37). Blue cord, gold plate, front of the turban. Anyone facing Aaron sees it first.

Look again, friend. The text says, "Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban" (Exodus 28:37). So the statement is true. The plate rides up front, held by a blue cord.

explanations.answer: So they may be acceptable before the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The plate "shall always be on his forehead, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD" (Exodus 28:38). It's tied to the holy gifts the Israelites consecrate. Aaron wears it for them.

explanations.answer: So Aaron may rule over all the tribes
explanations.explanation: Not what God says, friend. The plate is on his forehead "so that they may be acceptable before the LORD" (Exodus 28:38). Ruling the tribes isn't the reason given.

explanations.answer: So the people may never sin again
explanations.explanation: That's a big promise, friend, and the text doesn't make it. God says the plate is on Aaron's forehead "so that they may be acceptable before the LORD" (Exodus 28:38). That's the reason the verse gives.

Yes, friend. God says, "Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron's sons, to give them glory and splendor" (Exodus 28:40). Same words He used for Aaron's garments (Exodus 28:2). The sons get the glory and splendor too.

The sons aren't left out, friend. God says, "Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron's sons, to give them glory and splendor" (Exodus 28:40). So the statement is true. They get dressed for the job too.

That's it. After Moses puts the garments on, God says to "anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests" (Exodus 28:41). The clothes come first, then the setting apart. Both are part of the plan.
Interesting idea, friend, but it isn't in the verse. After the garments go on, God says to "anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them" (Exodus 28:41). Moses has more to do, and it isn't a parade.

Counting isn't what comes next here, friend. God tells Moses to "anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests" (Exodus 28:41). That's the next step after the garments.
That's the word. God says, "This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants" (Exodus 28:43). It isn't a one-time thing. It keeps going down the family line.
A calendar guess, friend, but not what the verse says. God says, "This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants" (Exodus 28:43). Permanent means no once-a-year schedule.
Opposite direction, friend. God says, "This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants" (Exodus 28:43). It's built to last, and it's meant for his descendants too.
